name: Numerical Precision / Exact Decimal Rounding
description: solution_code (Python) defines a solve(inputs, rounding_mode) function that must reproduce the curator's own precomputed expected_output BYTE-FOR-BYTE (exact string equality, never numeric/float tolerance) for a realistic financial/scientific/measurement computation -- compound interest, exact-cent bill splitting, currency conversion, per-line vs per-total tax allocation, weighted averages, and similar tasks whose entire point is that a float literal cannot exactly represent the decimal value being computed. inputs are curator-authored, as JSON strings (never float literals) for anything decimal-precision-sensitive, or plain JSON integers for counts -- so both the row's own authoring and solution_code's own computation can use Python's real decimal.Decimal type end to end. There is no independent oracle: unlike this registry's fixed-small-algorithm-set categories (rate_limiting_policy_simulation's 5 policy types, caching_strategy's 5 eviction disciplines), this category's computation varies arbitrarily per row, so expected_output is trusted directly (the same trust model diff_patch_application and data_transformation already use for their own curator-authored expected_final_content/output_data_sample) -- mitigated by this pipeline's own llm + human_audit stages, not by mechanical re-derivation. What IS mechanically enforced: solve() must return a decimal.Decimal or a str (never a bare float/int, so its exact string form is never left to an uncontrolled float repr), and a harness-computed perturbation of inputs (every numeric field nudged by a real, exact amount -- BigInt-precise in this file, never floating point) must make solve()'s own output change, so a solution_code that simply returns the literal expected_output string regardless of input is mechanically rejected.
executionEnv: python3 (stdlib decimal module only -- zero new sandbox dependencies). solution_code may use float internally for convenience, but its FINAL returned value must be a decimal.Decimal or a str; a float-precision bug that corrupts the final rounded value (e.g. round(2.675, 2) landing on 2.67 instead of the mathematically correct 2.68, a well-known IEEE-754 double-representation artifact) is real, valuable signal this category exists to catch, not something the harness papers over.

fields.label: Task description
fields.help: Natural-language description of the realistic financial/scientific/measurement computation, precise enough that a contributor reading only this field (plus rounding_mode and inputs' own key names) can implement solve() correctly, e.g. 'calculate compound interest, principal compounded `periods` times at `rate` per period, rounding to the cent at EVERY compounding period (not just once at the end)', 'split a restaurant bill total `bill_total` exactly `n_people` ways in whole cents, with any leftover cent(s) from the division distributed one-per-person starting from the first person, so the shares sum EXACTLY back to bill_total (no lost or invented pennies)', 'convert `amount` from one currency to another at the fixed rate `fx_rate`, rounding the converted amount to 2 decimal places', 'compute the tax-inclusive total TWO ways -- `per_line` (round each line item's own tax to the cent, then sum) and `on_total` (sum the pre-tax lines first, then apply tax once to the sum, then round) -- and return them as a JSON array [per_line_total, on_total_total] as strings, since the two are NOT interchangeable and may legitimately differ by a cent', 'compute the weighted average of `scores` weighted by `weights`, rounded to exactly 4 decimal places'. State explicitly which of inputs' own keys feed the computation and what rounding_mode governs (state it as prose too, even though rounding_mode is also a separate structured field below, mirroring rate_limiting_policy_simulation's own policy_description/policy_params convention of describing the same numbers from two angles).

fields.label: Rounding mode
fields.help: One of Python's own real decimal module rounding-mode constant NAMES (deliberately -- this string is passed VERBATIM as solve()'s second argument, so solution_code can hand it straight to Decimal.quantize(..., rounding=rounding_mode) with zero translation). ROUND_HALF_UP: ties round away from zero (the everyday 'round half up' most people mean). ROUND_HALF_EVEN: ties round to the nearest EVEN digit ("banker's rounding" -- the IEEE-754/many accounting systems' default, chosen specifically because it does not systematically bias sums upward the way ROUND_HALF_UP does over many roundings). ROUND_UP / ROUND_DOWN: always away from / toward zero, regardless of the discarded digits. ROUND_CEILING / ROUND_FLOOR: always toward +infinity / -infinity (differ from UP/DOWN only for negative values). AUTHORING GUIDANCE: for the mode to have genuine bite, prefer at least SOME rows across the dataset whose inputs land exactly on a rounding-mode-sensitive tie (a value ending in exactly ...5 at the rounding digit, e.g. quantizing 2.125 to 2 places) -- ROUND_HALF_UP and ROUND_HALF_EVEN only diverge from each other (and from a naive round()) at exactly such a boundary; a row whose numbers never hit one cannot actually distinguish a correct rounding_mode implementation from a solution_code that silently ignores this field and always uses Python's own round()-builtin default (also banker's-rounding-ish but NOT equivalent to decimal.ROUND_HALF_EVEN's own well-defined boundary rule) or a hardcoded ROUND_HALF_UP. This is authoring guidance, not a mechanically enforced gate -- see harness.js's own module doc comment for why a mechanical rounding-mode-divergence check was considered and rejected as too fragile a MECHANICAL gate (not every legitimate row's own numbers need land on a tie).

fields.label: Computation inputs (JSON)
fields.help: A JSON object, 1-20 keys, each key a plain identifier (letters/digits/underscore, starting with a letter or underscore). Every VALUE must be a SCALAR or a flat (one level deep, no nesting) ARRAY of 1-50 scalars -- an array covers a genuinely multi-value computation (e.g. `scores`/`weights` for a weighted average, a per-line `prices` list for a tax-allocation task) without needing a second, structurally different field. Each SCALAR must be either: (a) a STRING containing an exact decimal literal matching `-?\d+(\.\d+)?` (e.g. "1000.00", "0.05", "-12.5") -- NEVER a bare JSON number for anything decimal-precision-sensitive, since a float literal like 0.1 cannot exactly represent the decimal value 0.1 at all (it is really 0.1000000000000000055511151231257827021181583404541015625 in IEEE-754 double) -- this is this category's entire reason for existing, so the harness rejects a bare JSON float outright as a dataset-authoring defect, not merely discourages it; or (b) a plain JSON INTEGER (e.g. 12, 3) for a genuine COUNT (compounding periods, number of people splitting a bill, number of line items) -- never a JSON number with a fractional part, which is rejected as (a)'s float-literal trap under a different spelling. At least one scalar across the whole object (top-level or inside an array) must be a decimal-string value (a row using ONLY integer counts is not actually testing decimal precision at all). This object is passed to solve() AS-IS -- string values arrive as Python str (construct `Decimal(value)` from them directly), integer values arrive as Python int, arrays arrive as Python list in the same order. ANTI-HARDCODING: the harness independently perturbs a COPY of this object (every decimal-string scalar -- top-level or inside an array -- nudged by a real, BigInt-exact +10%-plus-one-whole-unit-at-that-value's-own-precision delta; every integer scalar incremented by 1 -- see harness.js's own module doc comment for the exact, deterministic rule) and re-runs solve() against the perturbed copy; its output must come back DIFFERENT from expected_output, or the row is rejected as suspected_hardcoded. AUTHORING GUIDANCE: keep every field genuinely load-bearing in the real computation (a decorative/unused key that solve() never reads cannot itself defeat the anti-hardcoding perturbation, since every OTHER field is perturbed simultaneously in the same pass, but an unused field is still dead weight worth avoiding).

fields.label: Reference solution (Python)
fields.help: THE GRADED ARTIFACT -- also this benchmark row's own reference implementation (this category, like diff_patch_application/data_transformation/rate_limiting_policy_simulation/caching_strategy before it, verifies that task+solution are a genuinely self-consistent, non-degenerate pair, not that a THIRD party's separate submission solves someone else's fixed task). Python code defining EXACTLY ONE top-level function named `solve`, with EXACTLY this signature: `def solve(inputs, rounding_mode):` -- `inputs` is the row's own inputs dict, passed through UNCHANGED (string values are Python str, integer values are Python int -- never pre-parsed into Decimal by the harness, so solve() must do its own `Decimal(inputs['principal'])` etc.); `rounding_mode` is the row's own rounding_mode value, passed as the exact Python decimal-module constant NAME string (e.g. use it directly: `total.quantize(Decimal('0.01'), rounding=rounding_mode)`). MUST return either a `decimal.Decimal` or a `str` -- returning a bare `float`/`int`/anything else is a real, mechanically-rejected structural failure (never a runtimeUnavailable), because a bare float's own str() form is not something solve() fully controls (missing trailing zeros, scientific notation for extreme magnitudes) and this category's whole contract is EXACT byte-for-byte string equality against expected_output. Internal arithmetic MAY use float if convenient -- this is not banned or statically scanned for -- but the FINAL returned value must be produced as an exact Decimal/str; a float-precision defect that corrupts the final value is a real failure this category is designed to surface (compared byte-for-byte against expected_output, never with numeric tolerance), not something the harness looks past. For a task whose natural answer is more than one number (e.g. a per_line-vs-on_total tax comparison, or a per-person bill split), solve() should return a single `str` that itself encodes the full structured answer (e.g. `str(json.dumps([str(a), str(b)]))`) -- expected_output must then be authored as the exact same literal string.

fields.label: Expected output (curator-precomputed, exact string)
fields.help: The curator's own hand- or tool-precomputed EXACT result, as a STRING -- e.g. "1051.16", never a bare JSON number (which would silently re-introduce this category's own float-imprecision trap into its own ground truth). Compared against solve()'s real returned value via EXACT STRING EQUALITY (surrounding whitespace trimmed on both sides; nothing else is normalized -- no numeric tolerance, no float coercion, and trailing zeros are SIGNIFICANT: "1051.10" and "1051.1" are different strings and this category deliberately does not treat them as equal, since exact cent/decimal-place formatting is itself part of the correctness contract most of these tasks care about). RESIDUAL, HONESTLY DOCUMENTED: this category has no independent oracle (see this schema's own top-level description and harness.js's own module doc comment for why one is not feasible here, unlike rate_limiting_policy_simulation/caching_strategy's small fixed algorithm sets) -- a curator's own arithmetic mistake in this field is not mechanically detectable and would wrongly fail an otherwise-correct solution_code; mitigated only by this pipeline's own llm + human_audit stages, the same residual this registry already accepts for diff_patch_application's expected_final_content and data_transformation's output_data_sample.
